extracted.intended_audience: young married women / housewives (late 19th‑century domestic audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for married women on domestic management, household finances, marital expectations, and methods for running a home affordably and respectfully. Emphasizes economy, method, mutual financial understanding, and personal dignity within marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not measure men by feminine standards of perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Men should not be idealized according to women's romantic or exaggerated standards; keeping realistic perspective prevents disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid canonizing a husband or construing ordinary traits (strength, slowness) as vices. Put him 'in his proper place' with perspective and common sense; recognize ordinary human frailty to guard against the shock of broken ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice noble reticence about a husband's faults
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventory of a husband's faults should be kept private and not subjected to carping public or domestic discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbearance, pride, and affection should prohibit public criticism. Discretion protects marital harmony; the wife's 'sealed book' of his faults preserves the relationship and honors his loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual understanding about ownership of family income
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear, mutual understanding regarding who owns and controls family income is essential to avoid heart‑burnings and contentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'right ownership' of income should be discussed and settled: whether the marriage vow implies gift or partnership, and how funds are to be managed so neither partner feels virtual pauperized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the wife with a stated household allowance and a personal sum
rubrics_metrics.description: The wife should receive a specified allowance for household expenses (to disburse herself) and a smaller but sure personal sum to appropriate as she likes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the allowance as a budgeted entitlement, not a gratuity; the household allowance enables proper management, while a personal sum preserves dignity and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize domestic labor as entitled to remuneration/partnership status
rubrics_metrics.description: A husband's recognition that his wife's domestic work is equivalent to paid labor justifies regarding her as a partner entitled to a share of the household's resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sensible husband should estimate what salary he can afford to pay his wife for house services and consider it a debt rather than a favour; this frames domestic work as contribution, not mendicancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absolute financial dependence; wives should own/hold something in their own right
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs that leave wives wholly dependent on husbands are unjust; wives ought to have bank accounts or property in their own right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership in the wife's name prevents 'conscious pauperism' and preserves dignity; husbands who fear a capable wife should be seen as unsuitable partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Husbands should communicate investment plans and earn trust
rubrics_metrics.description: If a husband invests funds which in effect belong to the wife, he should show and explain such investments to maintain her confidence and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency about long‑term plans and investments reassures the wife that her private fortune is being augmented rather than secretly absorbed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not glorify cling-and-dependence: independence preserves individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'cling-and-twine' model (wife as parasite on husband's resources) gradually strangles the wife's individuality and is dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate independence and competence rather than dependence; the object-lesson of the ivy strangling the tree warns against the parasitic model of marriage and household dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan house size and staffing to fit real needs and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Homes should be planned for those who live in them, not for occasional guests; a house too big for the family that lacks adequate servants causes overwork and ruinous strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid building or keeping houses that require more service than the family can afford; either employ sufficient staff or simplify domestic expectations—do not force the mistress into slavery to maintain appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy is not meanness; avoid waste
rubrics_metrics.description: Saving and avoiding waste are virtues—there is no meanness in economy, and waste is vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples include saving scraps of butter, leftover potatoes, and unused cream; such small economies materially help stretch limited incomes and are signs of good household management, not pettiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematize household work—method is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Method and management (system) in household tasks save time and money and prevent constant hurry and exhaustion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Housewives should develop routines and systems so work appears unflurried; good method allows time for reading, sewing, and other pursuits and prevents the 'always in a hurry' condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do some personal cooking and dish‑washing to reduce waste and breakage
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistress who does part of her own cooking and washes dining-room dishes saves money and reduces breakage while producing better, more delicate food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal involvement often results in faster, more careful work and fewer broken items than servants produce; with simple tools and hot water, dish‑washing can be a pleasant and efficient task for the lady.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use servants prudently and supervise them thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Using servants infrequently or employing too few (because of pride or pretence) results in overwork for the mistress; servants also require oversight to prevent waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where servants are kept, the mistress should supervise provisions and guard against theft or careless waste; hiring an adequate number of servants to match the household's demands is preferable to overburdening the family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pretentious entertaining but do not be ungenerous in hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagant, pretentious parties are to be reprehended, yet refusing common hospitality purely from stinginess is mean; welcome guests with what you normally provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be hospitable within means; explain quiet living arrangements to guests rather than altering the household for them. Do not invite guests whose presence would force major disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't let ambition for 'smartness' force unhealthy standards of living
rubrics_metrics.description: American ambition to appear richer than one is leads to buying larger houses and unnecessary furnishings, provoking overwork and false economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist fashions that compel keeping up appearances (parlors, pianos, expensive furnishings) when they exceed real means; such pretence pushes households into overwork, mental strain, and poor health for women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housekeeping effort should be ennobling, not degrading
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic chores are not degrading if performed with pride and the right spirit; they can ennoble when done with skill and thought of their meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small details (making good use of simple food, presenting a neat table) can transform scant resources into acceptable fare; take satisfaction in competent housekeeping rather than shame.
